title: Primitive modules: variable shaping, conditional interfaces, and upgrade playbook
body:
Purpose
This note captures design decisions and a practical upgrade playbook for primitive terraform modules used by private deployments (VPC, IAM, cluster primitives for EKS/GKE/AKS). Focus: how we shape variables/outputs and introduce conditional interfaces so we can evolve modules without forcing mass state surgery for downstream consumers.

Goals and constraints
- Backwards compatibility first: modules must not break existing stacks when we release non-major changes.
- Small, composable primitives: VPC, subnet topology, shared-services (NAT/bastion), IAM roles, cluster enrollment outputs.
- Cross-cloud compatibility where reasonable (export common minimal outputs; cloud-specific outputs are optional).
- Graduated rollout: experimental flags, feature toggles in module inputs, and a clear deprecation window.
- Terraform versions: support >= 1.2, prefer 1.5 feature set where possible but gate with conditional logic to stay compatible.

Principles for variable shaping
1) Flatten frequently-changed knobs to top-level inputs rather than nested map-of-maps for widely used options. Consumers should be able to override simple values without copying complex objects. Example: prefer "enable_flow_logs" over requiring a "logging": {"flow": {"enabled": true}} map in the common case.

2) Use typed objects only where a small set of fields always move together. If we expose an object, also expose a set of compatibility top-level inputs that map into the object (two-way mapping inside the module). This allows older consumers to keep using legacy top-level inputs.

3) Deprecation wrappers: when replacing a top-level input with a structured object, accept both and document precedence rules. Example priority: explicit new object > legacy top-level input > module default. Emit a plan-time warning via a "deprecation_notice" output if both are provided.

4) Feature flags for opt-in behavior: introduce boolean flags such as "enable_new_eni_strategy" so changes are non-disruptive by default. Default to false on minor releases; flip in a major.

Outputs and compatibility surface
- Minimal canonical outputs: vpc_id, public_subnet_ids, private_subnet_ids, shared_route_table_ids, cluster_security_group_id, cluster_oidc_provider_arn. Keep these stable names.
- Cloud-agnostic output set: provide a subset that every cloud primitive implements (vpc_id, subnet_ids, nat_gateway_ids optional).
- Cloud-specific outputs live behind namespaced keys, but we avoid returning nested maps as top-level outputs. Instead use suffixed keys: e.g., "eks_node_group_role_arn" vs "gke_node_sa_email".
- Introduce "compat_outputs" boolean that, when true, also emits legacy names (for migration waves).

Example variable compatibility pattern (pseudocode)
- input: public_subnet_cidrs (list(string), optional)
- input: public_subnet_cidrs_map (object): new richer shape
- internal: if public_subnet_cidrs_map != null -> derive cidrs from map
- else if public_subnet_cidrs != null -> use list
- else -> default to computed from availability_zone_count

This pattern ensures consumer stacks that still pass the simple list continue to work.

State migration and upgrade playbook (practical steps)
1) Preflight: add compatibility outputs and non-destructive flags in a minor release (x.y.z -> x.y.z+1). No resource renames. Publish release notes with explicit upgrade checklist.
2) Migration harness: publish a small consumer-side snippet (example stacks) showing how to adopt new inputs while keeping current ones.
3) Canary: enable new behavior behind flag; test in dedicated CI stacks (use short-lived workspaces in a sandboxed account).
4) Read-only verification: deploy consumer stacks with new module version and verify plan shows no destruction. Use terraform plan --detailed-exitcode and human review.
5) State migration (if renaming resource names is unavoidable):
   - Create new resources alongside old (non-destructive pattern).
   - Add outputs that map old resource IDs to new IDs so downstream can reference both during transition.
   - Provide a scripted state mv example in the module docs (exact commands) but only as a last resort.
   - Prefer resource aliasing (lifecycle create_before_destroy + new logical name) to avoid state mv when possible.
6) Deprecation: after a window (usually 2 release cycles / ~60 days), emit deprecation warnings and then remove legacy inputs on a major release.

Concrete terraform snippets to include in module README (text examples)
- How to opt-in to new ENI strategy:
  module "vpc" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@gitlab.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//vpc?ref=v1.7.0"
    enable_new_eni_strategy = false # opt-in later
    public_subnet_cidrs = ["10.0.1.0/24"]
  }

- State migration example (if absolutely required):
  # 1) take a snapshot
  terraform state pull > pre-migration-state.json
  # 2) move old resource to new resource name
  terraform state mv module.vpc.aws_subnet.old_name module.vpc.aws_subnet.new_name
  # 3) plan and apply

Testing and CI requirements
- Each module must include a lightweight terratest/pytest harness that exercises: create/destroy, upgrade minor, upgrade major (in CI sandbox). Test matrix should cover:
  - Terraform versions: supported set (1.2..1.5)
  - Cloud providers: aws, gcp, azure (where applicable)
  - Typical variable shapes: legacy top-level inputs + new object input combo
- Add a pre-merge automated plan check that runs terraform plan against a pinned consuming example to detect accidental resource renames.

Versioning and release rules
- Follow semver. Minor releases add non-breaking inputs/outputs/flags and are safe by default. Major releases may remove legacy inputs and will include a migration guide.
- A new minor must never delete outputs. If a name must change, keep the old output and mark as deprecated for at least two minor releases. Provide compat_outputs flag to emit both.

Operational guidance for SRE/Infra teams
- Keep a running inventory (spreadsheet) of consumer stacks and their pinned module versions. Automate reminders when consumers lag more than two minor versions behind.
- Maintain a Slack channel and a "module-upgrades" runbook where consumers can signal planned upgrades and request assistance for state mv.

Open questions and trade-offs
- How aggressively do we flatten variables vs encouraging structured objects? Trade: flattening reduces cognitive load for common consumers but increases combinatorial surface for arguments. We should default to flatten for the 80% case and expose a structured object for power users.
- Cross-cloud semantics: do we unify names for cloud-specific artifacts (node group IAM role vs node service account)? We keep minimal canonical names and prefer suffixes for provider-specific.

Action items (short-term)
- [ ] Draft module README template that demonstrates compatibility patterns (Asha)
- [ ] Add deprecation_notice output helper to the terraform module common library (Lin)
- [ ] Create nightly CI job that runs minor-upgrade plans for all primitive modules (Diego)
- [ ] Publish migration examples and state mv recipes to Confluence and reference in module README (Samir)

Notes to reviewers
This is intentionally pragmatic: aim for minimal disruption to customer stacks while enabling clean evolution. Please call out any patterns we've missed (e.g., secrets handling, provider aliasing corner cases) during review.

References
- Link to module testing checklist in Confluence: CONFLUENCE-PRIVATEDEPLOY-42
- Example MR with compat flags: gitlab.com/redwood/terraform-modules/-/merge_requests/87
